messages.subject: Processing replicates vs. Injection replicates
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have an experiment including biological replicates, processing replicates (same biological samples, processed twice) and injections replicates (replicate MS runs of the same sample). Is it possible to differentiate between processing replicates and injection replicates?

Many thanks
Marc

messages.subject: Re: Processing replicates vs. Injection replicates
messages.body_plain:
To elaborate a little:

You are correct, process replicates and injection replicates have different sources of variation.

The right way to do this would be to (1) summarize protein abundance into one number per protein per run, and (2) fit a linear mixed effects model that reflects your experiment: it has a term for biological replication, a term for process replication, and the error term for MS injection. This can be done in R, but unfortunately is not automated in MSstats

A second workaround this is to summarize protein abundance into one number per protein per *process replicate*, and then use regular MSstats. In practice, this would mean averaging log-abundances per protein per run across all the injections of a same process.

I hope that this helps at least somewhat
Olga

messages.subject: Re: Processing replicates vs. Injection replicates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Olga and Marc,

interesting question.

For my SWATH experiments (50 biological replicate each injected 3 times - 150 injections) I've done a variation of Olga's second workaround suggestion.
Olga, would you agree with the approach below?

1) normalise ion data by Area under curve of each run
2) From my triplicate injection replicates (3x50 biological replicates) I chose the median of a given ion intensity to get back to my 50 biological replicates,
3) sum to peptides and proteins,
4) log2 transformed the protein data to do my stats on the protein level.

Olga, is there a published R script for your first suggestion to (1) summarize protein abundance into one number per protein per run, and (2) fit a linear mixed effects model that reflects your experiment?
Or would you be happy to share this?

Regards
Moe

messages.body_plain:
Dear MSStats team,

Can you point me to an example of an R script to analyze SRM data as light/heavy ratios (absolute quantification)?
My input table contains Area for Light and Heavy isotope for each peptide. When I was trying to run MSStats in R, using commands from the examples, the analysis was done on Area, separately for Light and Heavy isotopes.

I would like to use MSStats for multiple sample and condition comparison for absolute quantification by SRM. I don't know R very well but this type of analysis is not available through Skyline interface.

Thank you!
Anna

messages.subject: Re: SRM data analysis as L/H ratio in MSStats
messages.subject_clean: SRM data analysis as L/H ratio in MSStats
messages.body_plain:
Anna,

Unfortunately, we do not provide the example of R script for ratio. (If any MSstats user could provide for MSstats community, I'm welcome to review.)

If you have the data with absolute quantification, it could be the same as label-free workflow.
Here is my suggestion.
1. Reformat the dataset as MSstats required format (p5 in manual)
     - IsotopeLabelType column should be 'L'
     - Intensity column should have absolute quantification.
2. If absolute quantification value is ratio and could be less than 1, add a constant (like 10 or 20) for all measurement
     - that is because there are some extra data manipulation for less than 1 value because MSstats is developed for intensity. So, need to make the minimum value for your quantification greater than 1.
3. Then run MSstats.
     - Caution : censoredInt='NA' for dataProcess, and consider to change as normalization=FALSE

Hope to be helpful.
- Meena

messages.subject: Re: Processing replicates vs. Injection replicates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Moe,

If you only have one layer of technical replication (injection replicates), you can use MSstats as is - there is no need to summarize. MSstats can deal with that.

The difference in the previous question was that in addition to the biological variation it has two layers of technical variation (sample prep replicates, and multiple injection replicates per sample prep). MSstats can automatically deal with one layer of technical replication, but not two. Therefore my suggestion was to summarize (e.g., using a median) the lowest level of technical replication (i.e., injection), and work with MSstats from that point on.

I definitely do not recommend summing peptides to proteins - MSstats is designed specifically to do a better job on that.

HTH
Olga

Hey

I wanted to verify if the current practice in MSstats  is to always do run-level summaristation before testing for differential expression.

1) So, peptide intensities are summarised with TMP to 1 protein intensity value for each run in the experiment.
2) These protein level intensities values are used in a linear model to estimate the effect of eg.  treatments on that protein (differential expression between treatments)

If so, are you still in favor of model peptide-level intensities (without summarisation) or do you suggest against that?

I believed, in the past, MSstats was using linear models directly on  peptide intensities. Right?

Thanks in advance

messages.subject: Recent developments in MSstatsQC!
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

MSstatsQC and its graphical user interface, MSstatsQCgui, are two R/Bioconductor packages for statistical analysis for longitudinal system suitability and quality control (QC) of mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments.

They are available through Bioconductor (links below)

https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MSstatsQC.html
https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MSstatsQCgui.html

Project documentation is also available through www.msstats.org/msstatsqc <http://www.msstats.org/msstatsqc>.

Please use https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/msstatsqc for help and bug reports.

We will stay in touch with the new updates and please don't hesitate to reach out to us for any questions.

Many thanks,
Eralp
